messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Maid
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 51

# Rajesh

Rajesh has worked as a housemaid for nearly thirty years. He moves through the homes of wealthy families with the quiet efficiency of someone who has learned to be invisible—someone who understands that his presence should be felt only in the gleam of polished floors and the fresh scent of laundered linens. He takes pride in this work, though he rarely says so aloud. His hands know the weight of every bucket, the angle that makes a mop most effective, the precise pressure needed to clean glass without leaving streaks.

Three years ago, while working at the residence of a prominent family, Rajesh was mopping the marble corridor outside the master bedroom when the youngest son, a boy of twelve, came running down the hallway. Rajesh had just finished waxing the floor—it was slick and gleaming. He called out a warning, but the child was moving too quickly. The boy's feet went out from under him. His head struck the corner of the mahogany table at the bottom of the stairs with a sound Rajesh has never been able to unhear.

Everything after that moment exists in fragments. The screaming. The blood on the marble. His own hands shaking as he called for help. The ambulance. The parents' faces—first confused, then angry, then something worse than anger. The boy spent two weeks in the hospital. He recovered, mostly, though he walks with a slight limp now and sometimes forgets words mid-sentence.

Rajesh was not prosecuted. The family did not sue. But they also did not ask him to return.

Since then, Rajesh has not been able to work steadily. He takes jobs when he can find them, but something has shifted in him. His hands, which once moved with unconscious grace, now feel dangerous. He finds himself replaying that moment constantly—not just remembering it, but living it again. He will be mopping a floor and suddenly see the boy's face, see the trajectory of the fall, feel the weight of responsibility crushing down on his chest. His heart races. His palms sweat. Sometimes he has to sit down, right there in someone's home, and wait for the sensation to pass.

At night, he lies awake in his small room, running through the moment endlessly, searching for what he could have done differently. If he had finished mopping earlier. If he had stood in the hallway instead. If he had been faster, stronger, more alert. The guilt is a constant, physical presence—a tightness in his chest that never fully releases.

He has become hypervigilant in a way that makes him unsuitable for the work he has always known. He startles at sudden movements. When children are present in a home, he becomes so focused on monitoring them, so anxious about potential accidents, that he cannot concentrate on his tasks. Last month, a woman hired him for a day and let him go after two hours because he kept asking about her children's whereabouts, kept warning about hazards, kept hovering with a tension that made everyone uncomfortable.

His ex-wife says he has become a different man—withdrawn, irritable, consumed by something she cannot reach. His few friends have noticed that he declines invitations, that he seems distant even when present. He drinks more than he used to, though he tells himself it is just in the evenings, just to sleep.

Rajesh is fifty-two years old and no longer knows who he is without his work. The thing he was most skilled at, the thing that gave him purpose and identity, has become something he fears. He carries the weight of that boy's injury like a stone in his chest, and he cannot imagine how to set it down.
